Autonomous field robots move into dairy farming

 30-07 | Crop solutions | Article

LinkedInFacebookXWhatsAppPrint

Joram Hofman is testing the Agxeed W4 wheeled robot over a longer period in cooperation with NPPL+R, manufacturer Agxeed and dealer Weevers Nieuwstad. Photos: Koos Groenewold

Autonomous field robots are often associated with arable farming, but they may also offer new opportunities for dairy producers. Dutch dairy farmer Joram Hofman is testing an AgXeed W4 autonomous robot for mowing, tedding and raking grass. Future Farming visited the farm to see how the machine fits into an already highly automated dairy operation and what role autonomous field work could play in forage production.

Whilst we take a walk around the farm, it soon becomes clear that the dairy farm is highly mechanised and, above all, highly automated. Several autonomous systems can be found in the somewhat old-looking sheds. At the front are 2 Lely A5 milking robots and at the rear of the shed there is a Trioliet feed kitchen. 2 Lely manure robots make their rounds on the slatted floors and all tractors are equipped with GPS and Isobus systems. And there is now also a new robot in the yard, the Agxeed W4, which the livestock farmer will test in cooperation with the Dutch NPPL+R.

Small-scale and highly autonomous

Maatschap Hofman & Van der Laan is based in Lytsewierrum (Frl.). Hofman runs it together with his girlfriend and father, and also sells surveillance cameras specifically for agriculture under the name Stalzicht. The entrepreneur also trades in second-hand GPS systems from John Deere. “The farm is not big enough for 3 people, but with the 2 additional activities we are busy enough overall,” Hofman says. The farm has 85 dairy cows, 53 hectares of grassland and milk production of around 9,500 kg of milk per cow. In addition, the dairy farmer carries out all field work himself, except for spreading slurry.

A robot tractor of more than 200 hp does not suit our farm management and our land

“We bought the autonomous systems, both the milking robots and the feeding robot, to replace my father’s work,” Hofman jokes. “My father is now 70 and wants to scale back a little. The robots mean he can take things easier.” Hofman also uses the data from the robots to optimise his farm management. “I have created an AI model that calculates the ration for the cows for me using the data I receive from the robots and the dairy,” Hofman explains. With the use of this system and the introduction of the feeding robot, Hofman has started feeding more efficiently. “I do not think milk yield has increased because of the feeding robot, but I am now using feed more efficiently,” the dairy farmer concludes. He also notices that there is much more calm in the shed. The only machines that still come onto the feed passage are the electrically driven feeding robot and mini loader, neither of which makes much noise. The cows have now become so used to that calm that, should a tractor drive along the feed passage, the cows and especially the youngstock are startled badly by the noise.

Raking and baling in 1 pass

When we look at the machines, 1 detail immediately stands out. 2 of the 3 tractors do not have a cab. “That is nice, is it not,” Hofman says. Hofman only works in the field when the weather is good, and then an open tractor is much more enjoyable to work with, the livestock farmer says. The second thing that stands out in the machinery shed is the rake on the front linkage of the John Deere. “My father always did the raking, but he is doing less of that now too,” Hofman says. To avoid losing efficiency, Hofman wanted to rake and bale in 1 pass. Hofman has had the combination since the 5th cut last year and is pleased with it. “Raking the headland is a bit awkward, so if it works out my father still does that with the normal rake. I can now rake using GPS without the bales being poorly filled as a result,” Hofman concludes. The rake is set up precisely for the baler, making the swath so wide that Hofman no longer has to weave with the baler to get a well-filled bale.

Before the robot can start mowing, the combination is made autonomy-ready. The robot drives in reverse, so the bumper is moved to the rear of the robot. For this, the mechanisation company is making a stand on the mower in which the mechanic hangs the bumper.The new robot on the farm

Alongside all the machinery and robots, Hofman has had a new robot on the yard since this week: the Agxeed W4. Hofman is testing this 4-wheel robot for more than a month in cooperation with NPPL+R and Agxeed. “I was also interested in the system from iQuus, but the tractor we could test had more than 200 hp and that does not suit our farm management and our land,” Hofman says. When the dairy farmer got talking to Agxeed during the NPPL participants’ day, the idea arose to test the 75 hp wheeled robot.

I am very curious to see how the robot fits within the machinery fleet and how much has to be adapted

Mainly mowing

The robot will mainly do the mowing work for the livestock farmer. After the first cut, Hofman always mows a small area at a time to stay in line with the cows’ grazing. For him, the test will be successful if he can put the robot in the field and it carries out the mowing neatly. “I am quite interested in the possibilities of a robot, but at our farm scale it is not viable to buy an Agxeed. This is a good way to become familiar with the technology,” Hofman says.

In addition to mowing, the dairy farmer also wants to ted and rake with the robot. He also sees the possibility of automating pasture harrowing and fertiliser spreading. “My spreader spreads using GPS and Isobus on the basis of task maps. Since the robot has an Isobus connection, it should work, but that will still be a small challenge.”

To make the mower autonomy-ready, a sensor has been fitted to the mower’s PTO shaft. If the PTO now stops rotating, the robot also stops. To ensure a good signal, rust is removed from the PTO shaft. Photo: Lucas van de WeijerIn addition to being technically able to carry out the work, the work itself also has to go well. “I now have to start thinking about everything that could go wrong and how that can be detected with sensors,” Hofman says thoughtfully. Together with dealer Weevers-Nieuwstad from Lelystad and researchers from WUR, the livestock farmer is looking at which sensors and modifications are needed on the machinery to allow the robot to do its work safely and reliably.

Working with autonomous systems is not new for Joram Hofman. A Trioliet feeding robot, 2 Lely milking robots and 2 Lely feeding robots are operating on his farm, and all tractors are equipped with GPS and Isobus systems.“This is the first time NPPL has tested an Agxeed robot in grassland cultivation and harvesting, so it is a bit of pioneering,” says WUR researcher Koen van Boheemen. “I hope the robot’s performance comes close to that of a human driver. Should something unusual happen, it remains to be seen whether it is the robot’s fault. Variation in the field and in the mower, or other machines driven by the robot, can also cause problems.” For Van Boheemen, the test is successful if the livestock farmer is satisfied. “I am very curious to see how the robot fits within the current machinery fleet and how much needs to be adapted on machines in order to use them reliably in combination with the robot.”

A rake is mounted on the front linkage of the largest John Deere. With this Samasz rake, Hofman can rake and bale in 1 pass. An important efficiency gain in the farm’s forage harvesting.

translationZh:
自主田间机器人通常与耕地农业联系在一起，但它们也可能为奶农带来新的机遇。荷兰奶农Joram Hofman正在测试一台AgXeed W4自主机器人，用于割草、摊晒和搂草。Future Farming杂志走访了该农场，了解这台机器如何融入一个已经高度自动化的奶牛场，以及自主田间作业在饲草生产中可能发挥的作用。

在农场里走一圈，很快就会发现这个奶牛场高度机械化，而且最重要的是高度自动化。在略显陈旧的牛舍里，可以看到几个自主系统。前面有两台Lely A5挤奶机器人，牛舍后面有一个Trioliet饲喂厨房。两台Lely粪污清理机器人在漏缝地板上巡回工作，所有拖拉机都配备了GPS和Isobus系统。现在院子里又多了一台新机器人——Agxeed W4，这位奶农将与荷兰NPPL+R项目合作进行测试。

**小规模且高度自主**

Maatschap Hofman & Van der Laan农场位于荷兰弗里斯兰省的Lytsewierrum。Hofman与女友和父亲共同经营，同时还以Stalzicht品牌销售专用于农业的监控摄像头。这位企业家还从事约翰迪尔二手GPS系统的交易。“这个农场对三个人来说不够大，但加上这两项副业，我们总体上很忙，”Hofman说。农场有85头奶牛，53公顷草地，每头牛年产奶量约9500公斤。此外，除撒施粪肥外，所有田间作业都由这位奶农自己完成。

“我们购买自主系统，包括挤奶机器人和饲喂机器人，是为了替代我父亲的工作，”Hofman开玩笑说。“我父亲现在70岁了，想稍微轻松一点。机器人让他可以更省力。”Hofman还利用机器人数据来优化农场管理。“我创建了一个AI模型，利用从机器人和乳品厂获得的数据为我计算奶牛日粮，”Hofman解释道。通过使用这个系统和引入饲喂机器人，Hofman开始更高效地饲喂。“我不认为产奶量因为饲喂机器人而增加，但我现在更高效地利用饲料，”这位奶农总结道。他还注意到牛舍里安静了许多。现在唯一进入饲喂通道的机器是电动饲喂机器人和小型装载机，它们噪音都不大。奶牛们已经习惯了这种安静，如果拖拉机驶过饲喂通道，奶牛尤其是小牛会被噪音吓到。

**搂草和打捆一次完成**

当我们查看机器时，一个细节立刻引起了注意。三台拖拉机中有两台没有驾驶室。“这很好，不是吗？”Hofman说。Hofman只在天气好的时候下地干活，那时开放式拖拉机更让人愉快，这位奶农说。机库里第二个引人注目的细节是约翰迪尔前悬挂装置上的搂草机。“我父亲以前总是做搂草，但现在他做得也少了，”Hofman说。为了避免效率损失，Hofman想一次完成搂草和打捆。Hofman从去年第五茬草开始使用这个组合，并对此感到满意。“地头搂草有点麻烦，所以如果可行的话，我父亲仍然用普通搂草机做。我现在可以用GPS搂草，而且不会导致草捆填充不好，”Hofman总结道。搂草机精确地针对打捆机设置，使得草条足够宽，Hofman不再需要为了获得饱满的草捆而左右摇摆打捆机。

在机器人开始割草之前，需要将组合设备调整为自主作业状态。机器人倒车行驶，因此保险杠被移到机器人后部。为此，机械化公司正在割草机上制作一个支架，机械师将保险杠挂在其上。

**农场上的新机器人**

除了所有机械和机器人，Hofman本周还迎来了一台新机器人：Agxeed W4。Hofman将与NPPL+R和Agxeed合作，对这台四轮机器人进行一个多月的测试。“我也对iQuus的系统感兴趣，但我们可以测试的拖拉机功率超过200马力，不适合我们的农场管理和土地，”Hofman说。当这位奶农在NPPL参与者日与Agxeed交谈时，产生了测试这台75马力轮式机器人的想法。

**主要用于割草**

机器人将主要为这位奶农做割草工作。第一次割草后，Hofman总是小块地割草，以配合奶牛放牧。对他来说，如果他能把机器人放到田里，并且它整齐地完成割草，测试就算成功。“我对机器人的可能性很感兴趣，但在我们的农场规模下，购买Agxeed并不划算。这是熟悉这项技术的好方法，”Hofman说。

除了割草，这位奶农还想用机器人进行摊晒和搂草。他还看到了自动化草地耙平和施肥的可能性。“我的施肥机基于任务地图使用GPS和Isobus。由于机器人有Isobus连接，应该可以工作，但这仍然是一个小挑战。”

除了技术上能够完成工作，工作本身也必须顺利进行。“我现在必须开始考虑所有可能出错的地方，以及如何用传感器检测到这些，”Hofman若有所思地说。这位奶农与来自Lelystad的经销商Weevers-Nieuwstad以及WUR的研究人员一起，研究需要哪些传感器和改装，才能让机器人安全可靠地完成工作。

“这是NPPL首次在草地种植和收获中测试Agxeed机器人，所以有点开拓性质，”WUR研究员Koen van Boheemen说。“我希望机器人的性能接近人类驾驶员。如果发生异常情况，还要看是否是机器人的问题。田地和割草机的变化，或者机器人驱动的其他机器，也可能导致问题。”对于Van Boheemen来说，如果奶农满意，测试就算成功。“我非常好奇机器人如何融入现有的机械车队，以及需要对机器进行多少改装才能可靠地与机器人配合使用。”
author: Lucas van de Weijer
